newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl defends sick pay reforms at union congress.
newsitem.headline: Kohl defends sick pay reforms at union congress.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl ventured into the lion's den of a trade union conference on Monday to mount a staunch defence of his government's decision to cut sick pay entitlements.
Greeted by a chorus of boos and whistles, Kohl told the DAG white-collar trade union the sick pay cuts were necessary to reduce labour costs and maintain German competitiveness.
He said his centre-right coalition had been forced to act over sick pay because unions and employers had failed to come to their own agreement on how to reform the system.
"There was no consensus," he told around 200 delegates in the eastern city of Magdeburg. "The government was obliged to act."
Under the new law, approved by parliament last month, employers are allowed to pay their workers 80 percent of their wages for sick days instead of the previous 100 percent.

Kohl said Germany could not afford to stand still and maintain its high labour costs in the face of economic globalisation and the spread of new technology which would have "enormous effects on Germany as an exporting nation".
"Everywhere in Europe, all around us, from Italy through Spain and France to the Netherlands and Sweden, radical decisions to change are being taken," the chancellor said.
But Kohl also said he had never intended the sick pay reform to be imposed on existing wage contracts, as several big companies such as Daimler-Benz AG tried to do.
The employers backed down last week in the face of huge protests by more than 100,000 engineering sector workers.
